items.q: What does this review cover?
items.a: The Wnt pathway is ancient and conserved and regulates cell fate, migration, polarity, neural patterning and organogenesis. Humans have 19 Wnt proteins. Downstream of Frizzled (Fz), signaling splits into the canonical (β-catenin-dependent) pathway and non-canonical (β-catenin-independent) pathways, which include Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) and Wnt/Ca2+.
items.info: Published in 2008, so it reflects the state of the field at that time.

items.q: Where does the name Wnt come from, and why does the pathway matter for disease?
items.a: Wnt fuses the Drosophila segment polarity gene wingless with its vertebrate homolog int-1. Deregulated Wnt signaling causes cancers of the breast, colon and skin, skeletal defects and birth defects, including the neural tube defect spina bifida.
items.info: Wnt proteins and antagonists are tightly restricted in space and time during development. Wnt signaling has also been implicated in stem cell renewal.

items.q: How is the Wnt signal received?
items.a: Wnts bind the N-terminal cysteine-rich domain of Frizzled receptors (10 in humans), which are seven-transmembrane proteins resembling G-protein coupled receptors. Co-receptors are also needed, for example LRP5/6 for canonical signaling. The signal passes to the phosphoprotein Dishevelled (Dsh/Dvl), which can bind Fz directly.
items.info: Dsh is the first cytoplasmic protein used by all three branches, and the signal branches at the level of Dsh.
items.concl: How Dsh channels signaling into each branch remains unclear.

items.q: How are Wnts modified and secreted?
items.a: Wnts are glycosylated in the ER and lipid-modified (palmitoylated). Porcupine is important for this lipid modification, and secretion is regulated by Wntless/Evenness interrupted and the retromer complex. Outside the cell, heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as Dally and glypican 3 bind and stabilize Wnts, limiting diffusion and modulating signaling.

items.q: Which extracellular proteins antagonize or activate Wnt signaling?
items.a: Antagonists include Dickkopf (Dkk), Wnt-inhibitor protein (WIF), soluble Frizzled-related proteins (SFRP), Cerberus, Frzb and the context-dependent Wise; the review describes them as preventing Wnt interaction with Fz or LRP5/6. Norrin and R-Spondin2 bind LRP5/6 and may activate signaling without a Wnt, while SOST binds LRP5/6 and inhibits it.
items.info: These inhibitors are tightly regulated in the embryo and likely create Wnt signaling gradients for patterning.

items.text: Not from the paper: the review groups all antagonists as Wnt-binding, but Dkk is generally understood to act by binding LRP5/6 rather than Wnt itself. Worth checking against a newer source if this distinction matters.

items.q: What happens to β-catenin without a Wnt signal?
items.a: Cytoplasmic β-catenin is degraded by a destruction complex of Axin, APC, PP2A, GSK3 and CK1α. CK1 and GSK3 phosphorylate β-catenin, which targets it for ubiquitination (via β-TrCP) and proteasomal destruction.
items.info: The hallmark of the canonical pathway is accumulation of β-catenin and its translocation into the nucleus.

items.q: How does Wnt binding inactivate the destruction complex?
items.a: Wnt binding to Fz and LRP5/6 recruits Axin to the membrane, where it binds a conserved sequence in the LRP5/6 cytoplasmic tail. This binding is promoted by phosphorylation of LRP5/6 by CK1γ or GSK3. Wnt also dephosphorylates Axin and lowers its cytoplasmic levels, and Dsh is recruited to Fz.
items.info: MACF1 may help translocate Axin to the membrane, but the mechanism is unclear. CK1 and GSK3 act positively at LRP5/6 but negatively at β-catenin.
items.concl: The resulting membrane complex stabilizes β-catenin by sequestering and/or degrading Axin.

items.q: What is the role of Dishevelled in canonical signaling?
items.a: Dsh is phosphorylated by CK1, CK2, Metastasis Associated Kinase, PKC and Par1, which probably controls its localization and partner choice. It has DIX, PDZ and DEP domains; DIX and PDZ are central for canonical signaling. Activated Dsh inhibits GSK3, which leads to β-catenin stabilization and accumulation.
items.info: Dsh also binds Axin and Fz.
items.concl: How Dsh is activated is still unresolved.

items.q: How does β-catenin enter and leave the nucleus?
items.a: β-catenin has no nuclear localization sequence, and its import does not need importins or Ran. It may piggyback on other factors such as Axin, which also shuttles. It also has no nuclear export sequence; export uses either RanBP3 together with APC (which has an NES) or a Ran-independent route through nuclear pore proteins.
items.concl: The import mechanism remains poorly understood.

items.q: What does β-catenin do in the nucleus?
items.a: It acts as a transcriptional co-activator, best characterized with LEF/TCF DNA-binding factors. Targets include organizer genes Siamois and Twin and oncogenes Myc and CyclinD1. Legless and Pygopus affect its nuclear retention and transactivation.

items.q: How does canonical Wnt establish the Xenopus dorsal axis?
items.a: After fertilization, cortical rotation moves Dsh and other Wnt components to the future dorsal side, stabilizing β-catenin there and forming the Spemann-Mangold Organizer. β-catenin/TCF activates the homeodomain factors Twin and Siamois, which drive organizer genes. Ventral injection of Xwnt8, Dsh, β-catenin or dominant-negative GSK3 induces a secondary axis.
items.info: Whether a ligand was needed was long unclear; Tao et al. (2005) showed maternal Wnt11 activates canonical signaling for axis formation.

items.q: How does canonical Wnt pattern the anterior-posterior axis?
items.a: During gastrulation the organizer secretes Wnt inhibitors (Cerberus, WIF, Dkk, Frzb), which keep nuclear β-catenin low anteriorly and higher posteriorly. This gradient is needed for head formation and neuroectoderm patterning.
items.info: Canonical Wnt also controls posterior and tail patterning and formation of heart, lungs, kidney, skin and bone.
items.concl: The authors note there seems to be no organ system whose formation canonical Wnt does not directly or indirectly regulate.

items.q: What is Planar Cell Polarity and how was it discovered?
items.a: PCP is polarity within the plane of an epithelium, on top of apical-basal polarity. It was found in Drosophila, where mutations in Fz and Dsh randomize the orientation of cuticle hairs, sensory bristles and ommatidia. In vertebrates it orients inner ear stereocilia and hair follicles and controls dorsal mesoderm migration in gastrulation.
items.info: Its defining feature is regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, and it appears to act independently of transcription.

items.q: How does non-canonical Wnt control convergent extension?
items.a: In convergent extension, polarized cells intercalate mediolaterally, narrowing the tissue and lengthening it anterior-posteriorly. Wnt4, Wnt5a and Wnt11 signal non-canonically, and their overexpression disrupts convergent extension in Xenopus and zebrafish without strongly affecting cell fate. Dsh, Fz, Daam1, Rho, Rac, Prickle and Strabismus also affect it.
items.info: PKA is a negative regulator: it binds RhoA and inhibits Rho without affecting β-catenin transcription. The pathway also acts later in neural tube closure.
items.concl: The vertebrate non-canonical pathway is likely equivalent to Drosophila PCP because the core components are the same.

items.q: Which receptors and co-receptors mediate PCP signaling?
items.a: The signal is thought to go through Fz independently of LRP5/6, although LRP6 has been shown to regulate convergent extension. Candidate co-receptors are NRH1, Ryk, PTK7 and ROR2.
items.info: In Drosophila it is still unclear whether a Wnt ligand regulates PCP at all.

items.q: What are the downstream branches of PCP signaling?
items.a: Dsh uses its PDZ and DEP domains to activate two parallel GTPase branches. Rho branch: Wnt induces a Dsh-Daam1 complex, and the formin Daam1 activates Rho via the GEF WGEF; Rho activates ROCK and myosin to rearrange actin. Rac branch: needs the DEP domain, is independent of Daam1, and activates JNK.
items.info: Daam1 binds both Dsh and RhoA, suggesting a positive feedback loop. Figure 2 adds that Daam1 drives actin polymerization through Profilin.
items.concl: Factors downstream of JNK, whether any genes are transcribed, and how the opposing Rho and Rac activities are coordinated remain unclear.

items.q: How does protein localization relate to PCP?
items.a: In Drosophila, asymmetric localization of Fz, Flamingo, Dsh, Strabismus and Prickle mediates polarization. In vertebrates it is harder to see; Dsh, Rac and PKCδ localize along medial and lateral edges of Xenopus mesoderm cells, and Prickle is anterior in zebrafish. In convergent extension cells Dsh sits at the membrane and in lamellipodia, and its asymmetric membrane accumulation is required.
items.info: Overexpression or knockdown of Dsh disrupts its membrane localization and mediolateral polarity. Lack of good reagents limits vertebrate localization studies.

items.q: Is non-canonical Wnt instructive or permissive for gastrulation movements?
items.a: Evidence from zebrafish suggests permissive: injecting Wnt11 RNA at the two-cell stage rescues the silberblick (wnt11) mutant, so localized Wnt11 expression is not required.
items.concl: The authors consider the question still open.

items.q: What defines the Wnt/Ca2+ pathway?
items.a: Some Wnts and Fz receptors release intracellular Ca2+ from the ER through trimeric G proteins. Wnt5a, Wnt11 and rat Fz2 release Ca2+ without stabilizing β-catenin, and this release is blocked by pertussis toxin and transducin α, which inhibit G protein signaling.
items.info: Calcium waves occur in gastrulating zebrafish and Xenopus embryos and are thought to matter for early patterning.
items.concl: It shares components with PCP but is distinct enough to count as a separate branch.

items.q: What are the effectors of Wnt/Ca2+ signaling?
items.a: Ca2+ activates PKC and CamKII. CamKII (and calcineurin, per Figure 3) activates NFAT to promote ventral fates in Xenopus. CamKII also activates TAK1 and Nemo-like kinase (NLK), which antagonize β-catenin/TCF. PKC regulates tissue separation in gastrulation through CDC42.
items.info: Figure 3: Dsh acts through PLC and IP3 to release Ca2+, and DAG activates PKC. Dsh also activates a phosphodiesterase (PDE) that inhibits PKG, linking cGMP to Ca2+ release.

items.q: What does Wnt/Ca2+ do in the embryo?
items.a: It negatively regulates dorsal axis formation, promotes ventral fates, regulates tissue separation and convergent extension, and later heart formation. Pharmacological block of Ca2+ release stops convergent extension in Xenopus. Convergent extension defects from Wnt5a misexpression are partly rescued by CamKII in zebrafish, and CamKII overexpression alone inhibits Xenopus gastrulation.
items.info: Dsh, through its PDZ and DEP domains, induces Ca2+ release and activates PKC and CamKII for heart formation, so it is part of this branch too.
items.concl: Wnt/Ca2+ acts as a modulator of both the canonical and PCP pathways.

items.q: What other Wnt branches were emerging?
items.a: Microtubule regulation via GSK3 and Dsh in neuronal migration and synaptogenesis; Ryk and Src in axon repulsion; casein kinase inhibiting Rap1 in gastrulation; Dsh and GSK3 regulating TSC2 to inhibit mTor in cell growth; Dsh, aPKC, Par3, Par6 and Lgl in epithelial polarity; PKA and CREB inducing MyoD and Myf5 in myogenesis; ROR2 controlling PAPC via CDC42 and JNK.
items.concl: How these branches relate to and integrate with the main three is obscure.

items.q: Does a given Wnt or Fz determine which pathway is activated?
items.a: Not simply. Wnt8 causes nuclear β-catenin but not Ca2+ signaling, Wnt5a induces Ca2+ flux but not β-catenin, and Wnt11 can activate both. Fz receptors also activate both branches, although rat Fz1 does not raise Ca2+ or activate PKC and CamKII in zebrafish, while rat Fz2 does.
items.info: Co-receptors may decide: LRP5 and LRP6 are implicated only in canonical signaling, while NRH1, PTK7 and ROR2 selectively transduce non-canonical signaling.
items.concl: Specificity is probably not set by a ligand-receptor pair but by co-receptors, Dsh binding partners and Dsh localization.

items.q: How do Dsh domains, partners and localization direct signaling?
items.a: The DIX domain binds Axin and is essential for canonical but not non-canonical signaling. PDZ works in canonical, PCP and Wnt/Ca2+ signaling. DEP works in non-canonical signaling and is needed for Dsh membrane translocation. Dsh bound to Daam1, Strabismus or Prickle (via PDZ) acts in PCP, while Dsh bound to CK1, GSK3 or GBP acts in canonical signaling.
items.info: About 30 Dsh binding partners were known. Removing Dsh from the membrane blocks Rho activation and convergent extension but not canonical signaling. Dsh shuttles into the nucleus, but the importance of nuclear Dsh is unclear.

items.q: What is the overall conclusion?
items.a: Two decades of work built a molecular framework for the main Wnt branches and cemented Wnt's role in embryonic patterning. But the integration, specificity and biochemistry of Wnt signaling are still unclear, and deregulated Wnt is strongly linked to human disease.

items.text: Recurring open questions in this review: how Dsh is activated and routes signals into each branch, how β-catenin enters the nucleus, what lies downstream of JNK, and whether non-canonical Wnt is instructive or permissive. Since this is a 2008 review, check newer literature before treating these as still open.

Wnt11 appears on both sides: it is a classic non-canonical/PCP ligand (silberblick, Ca2+ release) but maternal Wnt11 activates canonical signaling for the Xenopus dorsal axis. Good example for the point that ligands do not fix the branch.
